content:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-10-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Asha Singh (Pelion CTO), Liam Carter (Platform Eng), Rita Huang (ML Eng)

Auto-summary:
Redwood and Pelion reviewed pilot throughput metrics from the latest 24h run. Main focus was lowering 95/99th percentile latency while maintaining target throughput via continuous batching, queue shaping, and concurrency caps. Diego proposed a revised batching window and adaptive concurrency policy. Pelion agreed to run a night test with the v3 config and to add queue-depth instrumentation. Next steps and action items captured at end.

Topics:
- Throughput numbers vs expected baseline
- Continuous batching tuning (window sizes, max batch)
- Concurrency targets and throttling policy
- Queueing behavior and tail latency
- KV cache priming and warmup effects
- Risk of dedicated vs hosted fallbacks

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We have 48 minutes on the calendar. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Asha Singh: Hi, Asha here, Pelion CTO.
[00:16] Liam Carter: Liam, platform eng, quick hello.
[00:18] Rita Huang: Rita, ML eng on the latency side.
[00:21] Diego Ramos: Diego from Redwood SE.
[00:24] Maya Patel: Cool. We'll jump in — Diego, take us through the latest run results.
[00:30] Diego Ramos: Sure, so we ran the v2 config for 24 hours starting Monday night. Aggregate throughput matched target at ~1.2k requests per second sustained, but we saw tails at the 99th that spiked to 1.2s occasionally, and a small population around 2.1s during a brief backpressure event. The median token latency was fine, about 85ms per token with batching. The weird bit was queue depth correlation — when queuing crept above 40, we started to see latency tail emerge.
[01:10] Rita Huang: Just to confirm, those spikes correlated with a model switch event? I think we had a fallback to the small-quantized variant once the dedicated pool hit OOM previously.
[01:24] Diego Ramos: Good catch, we did have two automatic fallbacks during a burst on Tuesday morning. The routing policy fell back to the 7B quantized variant which has different kernel paths so cold KV cache temperature and different batch packing — that explains some of the variance.
[01:44] Liam Carter: Is that something we can pin or avoid during the pilot? We don't want model switching to muddy the throughput numbers.
[01:51] Maya Patel: You can pin model versions in the pilot config, yes. For the night run we recommend pinning to the main variant so we have clean baselines. For production you'd probably keep the fallback heuristics though.
[02:05] Asha Singh: For the pinning, is that a config flag we control or is it Redwood-managed?
[02:11] Diego Ramos: It's a customer-controlled rollout policy in the pilot runbook — we can show the exact flag. I'll paste the snippet after the call. (slight pause) Also, regarding continuous batching, we increased max batch size to 64 in v2; that helps token efficiency but increases per-request packing latency for single-shot requests.
[02:35] Rita Huang: We're mostly single-turn, low-context prompts; big batches don't always help us.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: Right, so the tuning we proposed is smaller max batch (32) with more aggressive latency-targeted batching windows — reduce window from 35ms to 18ms and cap batch at 32. That reduces the de-facto wait time for small requests.
[02:58] Maya Patel: And we can combine that with a concurrency cap per worker to keep queue depth lower. Diego, what's the recommended concurrency target for Pelion's workload shape?
[03:08] Diego Ramos: Based on your QPS and average tokens per request, we're recommending a soft concurrency of 10 per model shard, with a hard cap at 14. That keeps steady-state throughput high while preventing the queue from backing up when you get a conc of bursts.
[03:22] Liam Carter: What's the behavioral change when the hard cap hits? Do we reject or queue upstream?
[03:29] Diego Ramos: By default the platform will queue up to a queue-depth threshold; beyond that we have two options — return 429s to clients or route to a lower-cost fallback. For pilot, we suggest queuing plus early-shed with a progressively increasing 429 rate beyond the safety threshold so you can observe client-side behavior.
[03:49] Rita Huang: How do we instrument that in our client? We need histograms for queue depth and request wait time.
[03:55] Diego Ramos: We'll add a snippet to the runbook showing how to emit queue-depth metrics. Also, Redwood's tracing agent can capture server-side queue times — Diego will attach traces.
[04:09] Maya Patel: Quick note on KV cache: we saw a 15% improvement in median when the cache was warm; but the warmup period during scale-ups hit us pretty hard.
[04:19] Diego Ramos: Exactly — autoscale cold starts cause cache misses. For the night run we suggest pre-warming with a synthetic traffic burst before the ramp window, and a small holdback so the autoscaler doesn't spin up extra nodes mid-test.
[04:32] Asha Singh: Are there any security implications to the pre-warm? We run in our VPC(private) yeah.
[04:38] Maya Patel: Pre-warm can be done entirely inside your VPC. No data leaves your tenancy. For Private deployments we can provide runbook scripts that use local VPC IPs.
[04:47] Liam Carter: Can we also confirm KMS usage? Pelion needs all in use to be customer-managed keys.
[04:54] Diego Ramos: Yes, KMS integration is available in Private and Dedicated. For hosted we can integrate with customer-managed keys via partner KMS; Diego to include the KMS config notes.
[05:04] Rita Huang: Back to latency — those 2.1s spikes where they from lock contention or from request queuing?
[05:12] Diego Ramos: Mostly queuing compounded with the model-switch events; there were also a handful of RPC retries in the worker logs that elongated tail. I captured two sample traces — will attach.
[05:25] Maya Patel: For the config v3, what are the specific changes again? Diego, walk through the bullet list.
[05:30] Diego Ramos: Sure, v3 changes:
- Batch window: 18ms (was 35ms)
- Max batch: 32 (was 64)
- Soft concurrency per shard: 10
- Hard concurrency cap: 14
- Queue depth threshold: 40 -> early-shed starts at 60
- KV pre-warm: synthetic 5k requests over 3 mins before ramp
- Pin model: main-quant-v1 (no auto-fallback)
[06:05] Asha Singh: That queue-depth threshold change seems small — early-shed at 60, but you said our tails started at 40.
[06:12] Diego Ramos: Good point. The reason is we want some buffer; but we'll lower early-shed start to 50 for the night run. That should give you earlier signal without causing too many 429s.
[06:23] Rita Huang: Can we also try adaptive batching that reduces batch window under high queue depth?
[06:29] Diego Ramos: Yes, that's possible. We have a simple policy: when queue depth > 30, reduce batch window to 10ms and cap batch at 16. We can enable that as an experiment flag.
[06:40] Liam Carter: That seems promising — fewer tails and better latency. What's the risk of oscillation with adaptive batching?
[06:46] Diego Ramos: Risk is minimal if hysteresis is used — e.g., require queue depth to fall below 20 before reverting. We'll include hysteresis thresholds in the runbook.
[06:56] Maya Patel: Any other anomalies in the metrics we should call out?
[07:00] Diego Ramos: There were a couple of worker OOMs on one node due to an older kernel build; that's fixed in the latest runtime image. We recommend updating the runtime image before the next run.
[07:11] Asha Singh: Is that a rolling upgrade or will it cause downtime?
[07:14] Diego Ramos: Rolling, no downtime. It's just a recommended image tag replacement as part of the pilot preflight.
[07:20] Rita Huang: For the night test, what's the exact acceptance criteria we should use to decide if config v3 is a win?
[07:27] Diego Ramos: Suggested acceptance criteria:
- Sustained throughput >= 1.15k RPS over 4 hours
- 95th latency < 650ms
- 99th latency < 1s for >= 90% of the run
- No more than 1 model-switch event
[07:49] Liam Carter: If we fail those, what's the rollback plan?
[07:52] Maya Patel: Rollback is automatic — you can pin back to v2 via the control plane or we can revert the rollout. We'll also gather traces for triage.
[07:59] Asha Singh: About cost — you mentioned tradeoffs, do we have an estimate of additional GPU-hours if we tighten latency to hit 95th < 500ms?
[08:09] Diego Ramos: Rough ballpark is +12–18% GPU cost depending on batch packing inefficiencies. I'll send a cost/latency delta table after the call.
[08:18] Maya Patel: Let's capture the concrete next steps and owners. Diego, can you recap what you'll deliver by Friday?
[08:26] Diego Ramos: I'll send: updated runbook with v3 config, traces for the two slow tails, the cost/latency table, and a snippet for queue-depth instrumentation. Target: 2026-10-08.
[08:38] Maya Patel: Pelion team, you will run the night test with pinned model and post results by 2026-10-09?
[08:45] Asha Singh: Yep, we'll run the test, attach logs and queue histograms. Rita will own the instrumentation.
[08:51] Rita Huang: On it.
[08:54] Liam Carter: I'll coordinate the pre-warm schedule and make sure the runtime image is updated.
[08:58] Maya Patel: Great. One more thing — we've heard customers mention VertexAI and Lambda Labs in context of quantized variants; any final notes there?
[09:06] Diego Ramos: Just that different vendors have different cold-start behavior. Our debug traces should make it clear if kernel-selection or another factor is dominating. No action needed now.
[09:18] Maya Patel: Ok, wrap-up — we'll share the runbook and cost table, Pelion runs the night test, SE traces attached. Next sync — 2026-10-13 same time to review results unless we need a triage earlier.
[09:31] Asha Singh: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:33] Maya Patel: Thanks all. Bye.
